one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: South India-focused mass-market jewellery retailer under the "Lalithaa" brand, running 61 large- and medium-format stores backed by in-house manufacturing that lets it price gold jewellery at low value-addition charges.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Lalithaa Jewellery Mart Limited is a jewellery retailer operating under the brand name "Lalithaa", offering gold, silver and diamond jewellery designed for the regional preferences of southern Indian markets. As of March 31, 2026 it operated 61 stores across 51 cities in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka and Puducherry, over a total operational area of 650,881 sq. ft., selling only BIS-hallmarked jewellery. It backward-integrates through two manufacturing facilities in Tamil Nadu worked by 816 exclusive Karigars (plus 296 on non-exclusive short-term agreements), targeting mass-market and value-conscious consumers in Tier II and Tier III cities.

group_structure.title: Group structure (subsidiaries / JV / related parties)
group_structure.body:
- Asita Jewellery Manufacturing Private Limited — Wholly owned Subsidiary: Acquired in 2024 pursuant to the Asita SPA dated April 1, 2024; operates the Maraimalainagar, Kanchipuram manufacturing facility (approx. 20,000 sq. ft.) with 144 Karigars; respondent (with the Promoter) in a pending complaint by M/s Voice of Nature under the Water Act
- Centigrade Apparels Private Limited — Wholly owned Subsidiary: Acquired in 2024 pursuant to the Centigrade SPA dated April 1, 2024; has provided its land and building as collateral, and a corporate guarantee in favour of Canara Bank, for borrowing taken by the Company
- Lalitha Castle Private Limited — Group Company: Registered office at 32, Coats Road, T. Nagar, Chennai 600017; holds 420 Equity Shares in the Company
- Krishkiran Mega Mall Private Limited — Group Company: Registered office at 123, Usman Road, T Nagar, Chennai 600017
- A. K. Exports — Promoter Group entity (sole proprietorship of Promoter M. Kiran Kumar Jain): Operates in the same line of business as the Company and deals with certain common vendors; flagged as a potential conflict of interest
- Dilip Chhabria Design Private Limited — Deemed Promoter Group entity (Promoter shareholding more than 20%): Under liquidation; Company unable to access its accounting or secretarial records and could not obtain confirmations; SEBI declined the exemption sought under Regulation 300(1)(c)

cost_leadership.title: Supply chain integration (RHP report)
cost_leadership.body: Backward-integrated, asset-light retail model. Raw material vendors supply gold bullion, silver, diamonds and precious/semi-precious stones, which the Company purchases directly (gold bullion from bullion traders; diamonds mostly from diamond traders and sightholders) on the basis of tax invoices, through purchase orders and without long-term supplier agreements. The Company then supplies raw materials to Karigars (in-house and external) who manufacture jewellery to the Company's designs or designs approved by it, against making charges; the finished jewellery returns to the Company, is hallmarked and quality-checked, and is sold through its own stores - the Company describes itself as 'engaged in the complete value chain of the manufacturing process from designing of jewellery to selling of finished products'. Karigars manufacture more than 79% of products. Two owned/subsidiary Manufacturing Facilities support this: Thirumudivakkam, Chennai (approx. 43,861.96 sq. ft., operations commenced December 2, 2024) run by the Company, and Maraimalainagar, Kanchipuram (approx. 20,000 sq. ft.) run by wholly owned subsidiary Asita Jewellery Manufacturing Private Limited. As of March 31, 2026 the facilities are worked by 816 Karigars on exclusive arrangements and on the rolls of the Company (672 with the Company, 144 with Asita), plus 296 Karigars under short-term non-exclusive agreements. In-house manufacturing is stated to reduce jewellery-making wastage and allow lower value-addition charges to be passed to customers without compromising margins. Old jewellery exchanged or sold back by customers is re-used as raw material, and the Company procures old gold from customers to encourage repeat business. Quality assurance runs two checkpoints before a piece reaches a showroom - an internal quality control department checking purity and finish, then an external government-approved hallmarking centre operating to BIS norms; all loose diamonds are tested by a testing agency and all diamond products certified by an accredited laboratory; finished Karigar output is re-checked for gold, diamond and gemstone quality and design finish. Inventory is bar-coded at all locations and monitored manually and through the 'JILABA ERP' system which carries a built-in inventory management module and gives virtual connectivity across all stores and offices; stock levels are reviewed daily with replenishment action and supply chain is planned season-by-season. Inventory is carried at the lower of net realisable value and cost (annual weighted average cost for gold, silver and diamonds); as at March 31, 2026 gold inventory was Rs 86,830.29 million (Rs 868,302.9 lakhs), silver Rs 8,221.54 million (Rs 82,215.4 lakhs) and diamond and precious/semi-precious stones Rs 3,110.92 million (Rs 31,109.2 lakhs). Total inventory was Rs 98,162.76 million (Rs 981,627.6 lakhs) in FY2026, Rs 58,727.29 million (Rs 587,272.9 lakhs) in FY2025 and Rs 42,920.80 million (Rs 429,208.0 lakhs) in FY2024, with inventory turnover ratio of 2.55, 2.88 and 3.91 times respectively. Downstream, the model is asset-light: of 61 stores only three are owned and the rest are on leave-and-licence; distribution is entirely through own-brand 'Lalithaa' stores supported by in-house sales teams speaking regional languages, a customer-care mobile app, jeweller's block insurance on all goods movement, and insurance coverage at 81.04% of total tangible assets as at March 31, 2026. Working capital is part-funded by customer advances under the jewellery schemes (Rs 50,427.50 million / 20.15% of revenue in FY2026). Employees numbered 7,059 as of March 31, 2026 (senior management 11, managers 430, sales 3,979, security 195, administration 59, back office 1,222, others 1,163), with total attrition of 30.90%, 27.84% and 35.67% in Fiscals 2026, 2025 and 2024 (FY2026 by function: senior management Nil, manager 17.21%, sales 33.83%, security 16.41%, administration 38.98%, back office 35.02%, others 23.90%).

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Competition from both organised and unorganised jewellery retail (including online marketplaces) in highly competitive and fragmented southern markets, pressuring pricing, market share and marketing spend
- Expansion of the retail network and operations - store count moved from 53 (March 31, 2024) to 61 (March 31, 2026), with new-market execution risk around site selection, staffing, brand recognition and integration
- Exclusive arrangements with 816 Karigars in the Manufacturing Facilities, which reduce making wastage and let cost savings be passed to customers without compromising margins; retention of Karigars is a key dependency
- Cost of procurement of gold bullion - gold price volatility affects both consumer demand and operating costs; the Company does not use hedging practices such as gold metal loans, forward contracts or options, unlike most competitors, so it is exposed to major gold price fluctuations
- Product mix shift towards studded gold jewellery and higher-margin gold categories as a gross-margin lever, and towards silverware as a hedge against gold price hikes
- Working capital cycle driven by high gold and diamond inventory - inventory was 96.81% of total current assets in Fiscal 2026, inventory as a percentage of revenue rose to 39.23% (from 34.76% in Fiscal 2025 and 25.57% in Fiscal 2024), working capital rose to Rs 44,661.08 million and working capital days to 65 (from 56 and 50)
- Customer advances under jewellery schemes as a funding and demand-visibility lever - Rs 50,427.50 million in Fiscal 2026 (20.15% of revenue from operations), Rs 31,454.10 million in Fiscal 2025 (18.61%) and Rs 19,432.26 million in Fiscal 2024 (11.58%)
- Operating leverage from large- and medium-format stores - operating EBITDA per store of Rs 274.34 million in Fiscal 2026 versus Rs 123.39 million in Fiscal 2025 and Rs 128.33 million in Fiscal 2024
- Marketing intensity trending down as a percentage of revenue - Rs 817.86 million (0.33%) in Fiscal 2026 versus Rs 763.19 million (0.45%) in Fiscal 2025 and Rs 1,328.07 million (0.79%) in Fiscal 2024
- Seasonality - income and sales are subject to seasonal fluctuations around weddings and festivals
- Dependence on top three raw material suppliers, who contributed 58.03%, 67.20% and 66.98% of total cost of raw materials in Fiscals 2026, 2025 and 2024

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Expansion of presence and exploring untapped sections in southern and other regions of India, including 5 New Stores in Fiscal 2027 and 5 New Stores in Fiscal 2028 funded through the Net Proceeds, with further stores funded from internal accruals and other financing
- Strengthening presence in Tier II and Tier III cities and developing untapped markets for organised jewellery sales, positioning as a trustworthy alternative to unorganised players
- Expansion of the studded gold jewellery business, which carries a higher gross margin profile than other gold jewellery, including dedicated display counters (e.g. the Suchitra Circle, Hyderabad store)
- Prioritising higher-margin product categories within gold jewellery to continue increasing gross margins
- Expanding sub-brands and introducing new branded jewellery lines targeted at specific customer niches in gold and studded jewellery
- Expanding silverware and other lower-value product ranges to mitigate the impact of hikes in gold prices
- Increasing precious material ornament and design-centric jewellery sales through online promotions, digital advertisements and marketing, to optimise product mix towards higher-margin products
- Continuing to invest in brand building and marketing initiatives across print, outdoor, digital and below-the-line channels, and continuing to leverage the existing customer base through schemes similar to 'Free-yo-Flexi' and 'Dhana Vandhanam'
- Maintaining the asset-light, company-operated store model (all 10 New Stores to be company-operated, premises largely leasehold)

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: The Company intends to keep expanding its southern India retail footprint, which grew from 53 stores as on March 31, 2024 to 61 stores in 51 cities as on March 31, 2026 (8 Large Format, 43 Medium Format, 10 Small Format; 650,881 sq. ft. total operational area). From the Net Proceeds of the Fresh Issue it proposes to set up 10 New Stores - 5 in Fiscal 2027 and 5 in Fiscal 2028 - all company-operated, in a mix of Large, Medium and Small formats, with an assumed average store size of 11,000 sq. ft. The indicative cities are Chennai (2), Hosur, Kumbakonam, Viluppuram, Dindigul, Cuddalore and Nagapattinam in Tamil Nadu, Hyderabad in Telangana, and Belgaum in Karnataka; precise locations are not yet identified and no binding agreements for New Store locations have been executed as at the date of the RHP. The Board approved the 10 New Stores proposal by resolution dated July 28, 2026; premises will largely be leasehold with lease deposits and advance rentals funded from internal accruals, and any cost overrun above Rs 10,332.31 million funded entirely through internal accruals. On the manufacturing side, the Company commenced operations of its own Thirumudivakkam, Chennai facility (approx. 43,861.96 sq. ft.) from December 2, 2024, alongside the Maraimalainagar facility (approx. 20,000 sq. ft.) run by wholly owned Subsidiary Asita Jewellery Manufacturing Private Limited, opened in 2024.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Strong regional presence with deep penetration in high-growth South Indian markets, evidenced by 22.09% operating revenue CAGR between Fiscal 2024 and Fiscal 2026; South India accounted for a gems and jewellery retail market of Rs 5,026.00 billion in Fiscal 2026, about 40% of the Indian industry (Source: CRISIL Report)
- Highest operating revenue per store amongst key organised jewellery players in India, at Rs 4,102.28 million, Rs 2,816.22 million and Rs 3,167.56 million for Fiscals 2026, 2025 and 2024 (Source: CRISIL Report)
- Brand catering to the mass and value-conscious segment with own manufacturing (backward integration through two facilities and 816 exclusive Karigars), enabling low wastage and low value-addition charges
- Brand pull in Tier II and Tier III cities in southern India with focus on quality, craftsmanship and original designs; 45 of 61 stores in Tier II/III cities contributing 60.25% of Fiscal 2026 revenue
- Large Format Stores and Medium Format Stores driving scale: 8 Large Format, 43 Medium Format and 10 Small Format Stores as on March 31, 2026, including one of India's largest jewellery stores at Vijayawada (100,000 sq. ft. carpet area) and large stores at Somajiguda (98,210 sq. ft.) and Visakhapatnam (65,000 sq. ft.)
- Robust customer base owing to diverse jewellery schemes ('Dhana Vandhanam', 'Free-yo-Flexi', 'Jewellery Pre-Booking') with 473,412 customers enrolled and active as of Fiscal 2026, and the highest advances from customers among key organised players at Rs 50,427.50 million in Fiscal 2026 and Rs 31,454.10 million in Fiscal 2025 (Source: CRISIL Report)
- Asset-light retail model with backward integration, efficient inventory management and quality control: only 3 of 61 stores are owned, the rest on leave and license
- Highest ROCE in Fiscal 2026 amongst key organised jewellery peers in India, at 42.60%
- Templatised approach to store location, size and customer experience that enables scaling into existing and newer markets
- Long operating history since the first store in 1985 in T. Nagar, Chennai, with strong brand recall built around the Promoter's personal presence in advertising since 1999

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- Single-product concentration in gold jewellery — Gold jewellery accounted for 92.33%, 94.58% and 93.96% of revenue from operations in Fiscals 2026, 2025 and 2024. Higher international gold prices, higher import duties, regulatory restrictions, a decline in discretionary spending or a shift in consumer preference would hit almost the entire revenue base.
- Unhedged gold price exposure — The Company does not employ hedging practices such as gold metal loan facilities, forward contracts or options, unlike most of its competitors, so it is directly exposed to gold price fluctuations on both inventory value and demand. Jewellery purchases are discretionary and rising gold prices can cause customers to defer buying.
- Working capital intensity and inventory risk — The jewellery business requires substantial gold and diamond inventory: inventory was 96.81% of total current assets in Fiscal 2026 and 39.23% of revenue from operations (versus 34.76% in Fiscal 2025 and 25.57% in Fiscal 2024). Working capital rose to Rs 44,661.08 million and working capital days to 65; inventory turnover fell to 2.55x from 2.88x and 3.91x. Delays in inventory turnover or adverse gold/diamond price moves can force write-downs and stretch liquidity.
- Supplier concentration in raw material procurement — The top three suppliers of raw materials contributed 58.03%, 67.20% and 66.98% of total cost of raw materials in Fiscals 2026, 2025 and 2024. Loss of any of these suppliers or interruption in supply of gold bullion would disrupt manufacturing and store replenishment.
- Geographic concentration in five southern states/UT — All 61 stores across 51 cities are in Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Telangana and Puducherry, with Tamil Nadu alone at 53.98% of Fiscal 2026 revenue. Any regional economic, political, weather or regulatory shock, or region-specific competition, would hit the whole business.
- Dependence on Karigars for manufacturing — More than 79% of products are manufactured by Karigars; the Manufacturing Facilities are worked by 816 Karigars on exclusive arrangements plus 296 on non-exclusive short-term agreements as of March 31, 2026. Inability to attract, retain or replace Karigars, or competitors offering them better terms, would disrupt production and add cost.
- Reliance on customer advances under jewellery schemes as a funding source — Advances from customers were Rs 50,427.50 million in Fiscal 2026 (20.15% of revenue from operations), up from Rs 31,454.10 million (18.61%) and Rs 19,432.26 million (11.58%). This is unsecured customer money funding working capital; any regulatory change to deposit-like schemes, or a fall in enrolments from the 473,412 active customers, would strain liquidity and forward sales visibility.
- Leasehold dependence on store and facility premises — The Registered and Corporate Office, 58 of 61 stores as of March 31, 2026, and the Manufacturing Facilities are on leased or leave-and-license premises. Non-renewal, rent escalation or defective title would force relocation of stores whose location is central to footfall and revenue.
- Promoter concentration and related-party dealings — The Promoters hold 97.72% of pre-Offer capital and M. Kiran Kumar Jain alone holds 97.72%. The Company has related party transactions including brand ambassador fees of Rs 502.76 million in Fiscal 2024 paid to the Promoter, Promoter Group entity A. K. Exports operates in the same line of business, and Promoter Group entity Dilip Chhabria Design Private Limited is under liquidation with disclosures unavailable and SEBI having declined the exemption sought.
- Material tax and regulatory proceedings — A GST matter over allegedly excess ineligible input tax credit of Rs 533.17 million resulted in a January 8, 2025 order confirming the demand plus an equal penalty (total Rs 1,066.38 million); the appellate order of January 30, 2026 was partly favourable and a writ petition is pending before the High Court of Andhra Pradesh with a stay on collection of interest and penalty granted March 11, 2026. There were also 5 indirect tax proceedings (Rs 546.16 million) and 1 direct tax proceeding (Rs 14.19 million) against the Company, and a past income-tax search and seizure operation.
